t.2.2: Before them, the splendor of whose faces had faded, Brahmā appeared, as the radiant sun appears at dawn before lakes whose lotuses lie asleep.
t.2.1: At that time the dwellers of heaven, harassed by Tāraka, placed Turāsāh at their head and went to the abode of the Self-born Svayambhū.
t.2.3: Then all of them, having bowed down, approached with meaningful words the creator of all, the one whose faces turn in every direction, the lord of speech.
t.2.4: Homage to you of threefold form, who before creation were the Self alone, and who afterwards took on division for the apportioning of the three guṇas.
t.2.6: Manifesting your greatness through three states, you alone have become the cause of the dissolution, the preservation, and the creation of the worlds.
t.2.5: O Unborn One, from the unfailing seed that you sowed within the waters came this whole world of moving and unmoving things; therefore you are hailed in song as its source.
t.2.7: Woman and man are portions of your own self, for you divided your form out of the desire to create; those two alone are held to be the parents of creation, which partakes of birth.
t.2.9: You are the womb of the world, yet yourself without a womb; you are the end of the world, yet yourself without an end. You are the beginning of the world, yet yourself without beginning; you are the lord of the world, yet yourself without a lord.
t.2.8: You whose night and day are divided by your own measure of time: your sleeping and your waking are the dissolution and the arising of all beings.
t.2.11: You are fluid and you are hard through compactness, gross and subtle, light and heavy, manifest and unmanifest; in your mighty manifestations you have unhindered freedom of will.
t.2.10: You know yourself by yourself, and by yourself you create yourself; and by your own accomplished self you dissolve into yourself alone.
t.2.12: You are the source of those words whose opening is the syllable Om, whose utterance proceeds in three modes of accent, whose work is sacrifice, and whose fruit is heaven.
t.2.14: You are the father even of the fathers, the deity even of the gods; you are higher even than the highest, and the creator even of the creators.
t.2.13: They declare you to be Prakṛti, who acts for the sake of Puruṣa's purpose; and they know you alone to be Puruṣa, the indifferent witness who beholds her.
t.2.15: You alone are the oblation and the one who offers it, the food and the eternal enjoyer of it; you are the knowable and the knower, the meditator and that supreme object which is meditated upon.
t.2.16: Having thus heard from them praises that were true and touched the heart, the Creator, inclined to show his favor, replied to the dwellers of heaven.
t.2.19: What is this, that your faces no longer bear their own radiance as before, like stars whose light is dimmed by the mist?
t.2.17: Then the fourfold stream of words of that ancient poet, sent forth from his four mouths, fulfilled its purpose.
t.2.18: Welcome to you, O you of abundant valor, whose arms are long as yokes, who have arrived here all together, each upholding your own office through your powers!
t.2.21: And why has this noose in the hand of Pracetas, which enemies cannot ward off, sunk into the wretchedness of a serpent whose strength has been destroyed by a spell?
t.2.20: This thunderbolt of the slayer of Vṛtra, no longer casting forth the rainbow because its flames have died down, appears as though its edges had been blunted.
t.2.22: The arm of Kubera, a thorn in his mind, its mace cast away like a tree whose branches are broken, seems to proclaim his defeat.
t.2.24: And how have these Ādityas, cooled by the loss of their blazing heat, come to be gazed upon at will, as if they were figures set down in a painting?
t.2.23: Yama too, scratching the ground with his staff whose radiance has set, lends it, unfailing though it is, the worthlessness of an extinguished firebrand.
t.2.25: From the confusion of the winds the breaking of their force is inferred, just as the damming of a flood of waters is inferred from their flowing backward.
t.2.26: Even the heads of the Rudras, the horns of their crescent moons dangling from their bowed crowns of matted hair, proclaimed that their defiant roar of 'huṃ' had been crushed.
t.2.28: So tell me, my children, what do you seek from me, having come here together? For the creation of the worlds rests with me, but their protection rests with you.
t.2.27: You who at first held firm standing: have you now been set aside by stronger foes, as general rules are overridden by more powerful exceptions?
t.2.29: Then Vāsava urged Guru on with his thousand eyes, which shone like a lotus pond stirred by a gentle breeze.
t.2.30: Then Vācaspati, the two-eyed one, who was for Hari an eye surpassing his thousand eyes, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words to the lotus-seated one.
t.2.32: Emboldened by the boon obtained from you, the great asura named Tāraka has risen up like a comet for the ruin of the worlds.
t.2.31: O Bhagavan, it is as you have said: our station has been seized by enemies. How could you not know it, O Lord, you whose self is placed within each and every being?
t.2.33: In his city the sun spreads only as much heat as is needed to make the lotuses in the long garden pools unfold.
t.2.34: The moon serves him at all times with all its digits; it withholds only that single crescent which has been made the crest-jewel of Hara.
t.2.35: In his pleasure-garden the wind, its motion held back for fear of being charged with stealing flowers, blows beside him no more strongly than the breeze of a palm-leaf fan.
t.2.36: Abandoning their custom of serving in turn, the seasons, all intent on gathering flowers, wait upon him together just like ordinary garden-keepers.
t.2.38: And at night the serpents, led by Vāsuki, the jewels on their crests blazing, become steady lamps and wait upon him in attendance.
t.2.37: The lord of rivers anxiously waits within his waters for the jewels fit to be offered as gifts to him, until they have fully ripened.
t.2.39: Even Indra, hoping for favor to be shown by him, repeatedly seeks to win him over with ornaments from the wish-granting tree, conveyed by messengers.
t.2.40: Even though he is propitiated in this way, he torments the three worlds; a wicked man is subdued by retaliation, not by kindness.
t.2.41: By him the trees of Nandana, whose tender shoots the hands of the immortals' wives once plucked with gentle compassion, are now made to know the fall of the axe's cutting strokes.
t.2.42: For as he sleeps he is fanned with chowries by the captive women of the gods, chowries whose breezes mingle with their sighs and which shed a spray of tears.
t.2.43: Uprooting the peaks of Meru, worn smooth by the hooves of the Sun's horses, he has fashioned them into pleasure-hills in his own mansions.
t.2.44: Of the Mandākinī only a remnant of water is left, muddied by the rut-fluid of the elephants of the quarters; the golden lotuses that once grew there now have his pleasure-ponds as their home.
t.2.45: The heaven-dwellers no longer enjoy the delight of gazing upon the worlds, for the path of their celestial chariots has become deserted out of fear of his onslaught.
t.2.46: At the sacrifices spread out far and wide, that wily one snatches from the very mouth of Jātavedas the oblation gathered by the sacrificers, while we look on.
t.2.47: And by him was carried off the lofty Uccaiḥśravas, the jewel among horses, as though it were Indra's fame, won over a long time, given bodily form.
t.2.48: Against that cruel one all our means have had their workings thwarted, just as medicines fail against a virulent disorder arising from the combined derangement of all three humors.
t.2.49: And that discus of Hari, in which lay our hope of victory, with flames flaring up from the impact, only set upon his throat what seemed a golden necklace.
t.2.50: His elephants, having vanquished the Airāvatas, now practise their bank-butting tusk-blows upon the clouds, Puṣkarāvartaka and the rest.
t.2.52: Him, the protector of the armies of the gods, placing whom at the forefront Gotrabhid will bring back from the enemies the splendor of victory, like a captive woman.
t.2.51: Therefore, O Lord, we desire a general created for his subjugation, just as those who seek liberation desire the dharma that severs the bonds of karma, for the ending of worldly existence.
t.2.53: When that speech had come to an end, Ātmabhū, the Self-born, sent forth his voice, which in its gracious charm surpassed the rain that follows close upon the thunder.
t.2.54: Your desire will be fulfilled; let some time be awaited. But I will not myself undertake the work of creation for its accomplishment.
t.2.55: That Daitya obtained his glory from me, so he does not deserve destruction from me. Even a poison tree, once one has nurtured it, it is not fitting to cut it down oneself.
t.2.56: This very thing was chosen by him long ago, and it was promised to him by me; for by the boon his austerity was calmed, an austerity capable of burning up the worlds.
t.2.57: When he rises up in battle, skilled in war as he is, who could withstand him, except a portion of the seed of Nīlalohita once it has been shed?
t.2.59: Therefore you, by means of Umā's beauty, must strive to draw toward her the mind of Śambhu, held motionless by self-restraint, as iron is drawn by a lodestone.
t.2.58: For that god is the supreme light, established beyond darkness, and the abundance of his power has been fathomed neither by me nor by Viṣṇu.
t.2.60: Only two are able to bear the seed that the two of us deposit: she can bear Śambhu's, or his watery form can bear mine.
t.2.62: Having thus spoken to the gods, the Source of the Universe vanished; and they too, having fixed in their minds what was to be done, returned to heaven.
t.2.61: That son of Śitikaṇṭha, having taken up the command of your armies, will by the splendors of his valor loosen the braids of the captive women of the gods.
t.2.63: Having settled upon Kandarpa for that task, Pākaśāsana went to him in thought, with a mind whose speed was doubled by his eagerness to see the work accomplished.
t.2.64: Then the flower-bowed god, hanging on his neck, which bore the imprint of Rati's bracelet, his bow whose tips were as lovely as the playful creeper-like brows of women, and having placed his mango-sprout arrow in the hand of his companion Madhu, approached Śatamakha with joined palms.
